Hims & Hers introduces upcoming peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it announced the newly introduced products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the newly introduced products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October introduced an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a manufacturer spokesperson said in a statement.

According to recent reports, none of the tech giant's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims mentioned they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

Sources indicate that the company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Industry observers note that hims stated it aims to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The manufacturer also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized initiative to their needs, if appropriate.

The firm said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

It has been revealed that "If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori stated there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he remarked. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He remarked Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

Industry observers note that but health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," mentioned Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer noted the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Recent findings suggest that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, noted Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide consumers, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

Industry observers note that "With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

Sources indicate that but he stated the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The organization says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

In a recent development, hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that notes the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In a recent development, in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

According to recent reports, HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "substantial fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

In a recent development, there is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data indicates only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione indicated that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

Industry News: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a fresh study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.
  • Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes.
  • Recent findings suggest that mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a fresh study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.

Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes. They detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many contained multiple toxins.

Recent findings suggest that mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

According to recent reports, the investigation was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University. The researchers analyzed 212 products, including plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs). The selection covered foods commonly found on supermarket shelves, such as vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

Recent findings suggest that although the findings highlight how widespread these naturally occurring contaminants can be, the researchers also identified an important reassuring detail. Every product contained mycotoxin concentrations below recommended European Union guideline levels, which the team said reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

Why Plant-Based Foods Can Contain Fungal Toxins.

Many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination. Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mold in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

Recent findings suggest that unlike bacteria or viruses, mycotoxins are chemical substances produced by certain fungi. Their presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mold, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe. The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

In a recent development, this distinction is especially important for people who eat plant-based products frequently. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter these substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Could Repeated Exposure Pose Health Risks?

While the concentrations detected in the UK products were below recommended EU guidelines, researchers say the potential effects of repeated exposure deserve closer attention.

Earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks. In other words, assessing a single product may not provide a complete picture of a person's overall dietary exposure.

It has been revealed that eating one of these products occasionally is unlikely to cause problems based on the levels reported. However, a diet that relies heavily or exclusively on plant-based foods could involve repeated exposure to mycotoxins from numerous ingredients and products. Researchers say understanding the combined effects is crucial for evaluating possible long-term health consequences.

In a recent development, the severity of mycotoxin exposure varies depending on the compounds involved and the amount consumed. At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

The upcoming findings do not establish that the tested products cause these conditions. Instead, they provide information that scientists can use to estimate how much exposure consumers may receive through their diets and develop more accurate food safety risk assessments for the UK population.

Scientists Call for Better Monitoring of Plant-Based Ingredients.

Andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, emphasized that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet. Mycology is the branch of biology devoted to studying fungi, including molds and yeasts.

Recent findings suggest that "Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

However, a significant concern arises when latest foods enter the market, as there are right now no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organizations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.

In a recent development, we are currently collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers.".

The researchers are particularly interested in how food safety monitoring can keep pace with the growing range of plant-based products. Foods made from multiple ingredients present additional challenges because each component may introduce different contaminants, making overall exposure more difficult to assess.

In a recent development, their work also underscores the importance of monitoring raw materials throughout the food production process. Identifying and controlling contamination before ingredients are combined into finished products could help manufacturers manage potential risks more effectively.

What the Findings Mean for Plant-Based Diets.

The discovery of fungal toxins in all 212 products highlights the importance of studying dietary exposure across multiple foods, rather than evaluating each product in isolation.

In a recent development, for consumers, the results are not a reason to abandon vegan or vegetarian foods. The concentrations measured were below recommended EU guidelines, and the researchers stress that mycotoxins cannot be completely eliminated from the food supply.

Sources indicate that instead, the study points to the need for continued research into how different eating habits influence exposure, particularly among people who depend heavily on plant-based products. The University of Parma and Cranfield University are continuing their collaboration to investigate these dietary patterns, identify potentially vulnerable groups, and provide evidence that can inform future food safety policies.

The research, titled "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," was published in the journal Food Control.

The study was conducted as part of the European Union-funded Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03), Grant Agreement No 101079173.

#70490. Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1539 w)

Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A latest approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments.
  • It has been revealed that in experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A latest approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

It has been revealed that in experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic.

Industry observers note that over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

Despite these benefits, the medications have crucial limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

Berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

This process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

It has been revealed that "Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second.".

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle.

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

At the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

In mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an notable benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

Industry observers note that perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is important for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

How TOFA Increases Energy Burning by 18%.

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the fresh research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

Industry observers note that the compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

Other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

The Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

These receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

In mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," stated study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively.".

To understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

Surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an vital part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

These medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

It has been revealed that when the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär remarked.

In other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed.

Despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

According to recent reports, to help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology company called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

Recent findings suggest that if the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an crucial addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Sources indicate that additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
  • In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
  • Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, remarked it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

Recent findings suggest that "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot.".

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation.".

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

In a recent development, china's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security.".

PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those upcoming technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In a recent development, in Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000.".

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the glitch isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany.".

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

  • Industry observers note that A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX set a newly introduced record with its latest satellite launch out of California.

Industry observers note that A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov. 22) at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California), on a mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) called NROL-136.

It has been revealed that it was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force. And that quick turnaround made history.

Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn! 🏎️🚀🏎️🚀November 22, 2026.

"Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn!" Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX's vice president of launch, mentioned via X on Sunday. (Pad 40 is at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.).

Recent findings suggest that NROL-136 was the sixth launch of 2026 so far for the NRO. All of them have been carried out by SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, and all have delivered classified satellites to low Earth orbit.

The launch marked another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe.

About two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch.

Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the Space Force, and eight Starlink missions.

Sources indicate that NROL-136 was the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space, according to the NRO's mission website.

Recent findings suggest that the NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026.

As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 with the news that NROL-136 set a upcoming record for the shortest time between two debuts from the same pad.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the automaker remarked Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.
  • In a recent development, the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

According to recent reports, the automaker remarked Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

In a recent development, the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

Recent findings suggest that the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Sources indicate that alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, remarked licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

Industry observers note that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke mentioned Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

In a recent development, ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Industry observers note that ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the firm's energy storage business. Ford has noted the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

Breaking: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite.
  • Recent findings suggest that the study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution.
  • In a recent development, that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. Fresh research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

Recent findings suggest that the study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

In a recent development, that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn.

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

According to recent reports, however, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Industry observers note that each new fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

It has been revealed that dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle said.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record.".

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors.

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

Recent findings suggest that A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

Industry observers note that an crucial concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

Industry observers note that this approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans.

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

In a recent development, together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

In a recent development, as a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution.

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species currently classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

In a recent development, the idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

Industry observers note that such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever newly introduced fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

In a recent development, the proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as new evidence has accumulated.

Recent findings suggest that "The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle mentioned.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups.".

In a recent development, ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a strategy to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank.

Tucker remarked the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”.

He noted the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”.

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

It has been revealed that quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”.

Pressed later by a shareholder on the matter, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Industry observers note that investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”.

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who stated he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out aims for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”.

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”.

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

Sources indicate that the insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how promptly the deal came together.

According to recent reports, “Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” mentioned Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech.

According to recent reports, quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies.
  • In a recent development, the study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted.
  • To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

In a recent development, the study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders.

Industry observers note that previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

The University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

Recent findings suggest that "There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum noted.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

It has been revealed that "These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum mentioned. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet.".

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases.

According to recent reports, before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several notable questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

Despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery.

Recent findings suggest that for McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum remarked.

McCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Sources indicate that although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

Recent findings suggest that "It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he noted. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.".

#70475. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1441 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • According to recent reports, the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

According to recent reports, the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

Industry observers note that it also creates upcoming opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal Newly introduced Physics.

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

According to recent reports, when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

In a recent development, the upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Sources indicate that professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering upcoming technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most key components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

Recent findings suggest that this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from right now unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

It has been revealed that for now, the latest measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

Recent findings suggest that "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of fresh physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

According to recent reports, researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to vital advances in understanding nature.

"This is an crucial result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful latest way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

In a recent development, another batch of Amazon internet satellites will fly on Monday morning (Nov. 23), just eight days after a launch failure doomed 40 of the spacecraft.

Sources indicate that an Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation is scheduled to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana on Monday, during a 29-minute window that opens at 6:09 a.m. EST (1109 GMT; 8:09 a.m. local time in Kourou).

In a recent development, you can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of Arianespace, the French company that operates the Ariane 6. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Sources indicate that ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's Newly introduced Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And Fresh Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

Industry observers note that the Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

Monday's mission will be the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year.
